articles.title: Gold FoF inflows face curbs: What should investors do now?
articles.text: Several mutual fund houses have temporarily stopped accepting fresh investments into gold fund-of-funds (FoFs), leaving investors wondering whether they can continue investing through existing SIPs and what alternatives are available. Here is what the restrictions mean and what investors can do if they still want exposure to gold.WHAT ARE GOLD FUND-OF-FUNDS (FOFs), AND HOW DO THEY WORK?Gold FoFs are mutual fund schemes that invest in Gold ETFs rather than buying physical gold directly.When an investor puts money into a Gold FoF, the fund manager uses that money to purchase units of a Gold ETF. The Gold ETF, in turn, invests in physical gold. As a result, a Gold FoF’s value generally moves in line with gold prices.They offer a simple way to invest in gold through the mutual fund route without needing a demat account. Investors can buy and redeem units like any other mutual fund scheme while gaining exposure to changes in gold prices.WHY HAVE SOME MUTUAL FUND HOUSES RESTRICTED FRESH INVESTMENTS IN GOLD FOFs?Several fund houses have temporarily stopped accepting fresh investments in Gold FoFs from mid-October. The restrictions include fresh lump-sum investments, new SIP registrations and switch-ins, though they differ across schemes.While fund houses have not disclosed specific reasons behind the move, industry participants believe it may be linked to concerns over rising gold imports and strong inflows into gold investment products. As these ETF units are backed by physical gold, sustained inflows into such products can translate into higher demand for imported gold.Read more: Best gilt mutual funds to invest in October 2026CAN’T INVEST IN A GOLD FOF? WHAT ARE THE OTHER OPTIONS?Gold ETFs are one of the closest alternatives for investors seeking exposure to gold through market-linked investments. While there are restrictions on fresh investments in several Gold FoFs, there are none on their ETFs.Read more: Top 8 equity MFs offer double-digit gains on SIP investments since last Diwali. Do you own any?HOW ARE GOLD ETFs DIFFERENT FROM GOLD FOFs?Gold FoFs are generally more convenient for retail investors because they can be bought and redeemed like any other mutual fund scheme without requiring a demat account. Gold ETFs can only be bought and sold through a demat and trading account.Gold ETFs typically have lower costs because investors bear only the ETF’s expense ratio. In a Gold FoF, investors indirectly bear the expenses of both the FoF and the underlying ETF.Liquidity also differs. Gold ETFs can be bought and sold on stock exchanges during market hours, while Gold FoFs are purchased and redeemed at the day’s closing net asset value (NAV), like regular mutual funds.However, unlike Gold FoFs, their ETFs do not offer the convenience of a mutual fund SIP. Though many brokers have SIP facilities for buying ETFs and stocks, they are perceived to be relatively less user-friendly. Also, not all ETFs are liquid. Some of them might be trading at a premium to the ETF’s NAV.

articles.text:
United Launch Alliance announced Wednesday it plans to return its Vulcan rocket to service on November 13, nine months after a solid rocket booster anomaly threw the company's 2026 launch schedule into oblivion.

The return-to-flight mission will launch 40 satellites for the Amazon Leo broadband constellation, the first of 38 Vulcan flights Amazon has booked to deploy the bulk of its network. The mission will lift off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, and ULA said the launch date is pending range approval.

The launch is critical for ULA after its new flagship rocket suffered nozzle failures on its solid rocket boosters on two of its first four missions, most recently during a flight in February. In both cases, the rocket overcame the nozzle failure and completed its mission, but officials at the US Space Force, ULA's primary customer, lost confidence in Vulcan.

articles.title: Peptide peddlers cheer as RFK Jr. unilaterally grants access, overruling FDA
articles.text:
Anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy has unilaterally passed a rule that will allow specialty pharmacies to sell six specific peptide drugs, overruling scientists at the Food and Drug Administration.

The peptides are popular among members of Kennedy's Make America Health Again movement and many prominent MAHA figures and Kennedy allies sell them. Kennedy said he uses some of the peptides and called himself a "big fan." But FDA scientists continue to say there is insufficient evidence to show if they're effective and they are potentially dangerous. In 2023, the safety concerns led the FDA to remove the six peptides from a list of drugs that can be made by specialty pharmacies called compounding pharmacies—which make customized formulations of drugs for patients, or, in cases such as this, specialty drugs in bulk.

Kennedy's new rule sidesteps the need to formally undo that FDA action. The rule is titled "Enforcement Discretion Policy Regarding 503A Compounding Using Certain Peptide Bulk Drug Substances" and was made available Wednesday on the Federal Register, with the final publication data set for October 30. The rule does not change the regulatory status of the peptide; instead, it states the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) will no longer take enforcement action against compounding pharmacies for making the peptides, essentially giving them a green light to freely produce and sell them. Kennedy had quietly proposed this rule earlier this month.

articles.title: Jio Platforms lists on NSE as 3,138th company, making Ambani family proud with a 21.36% surge
articles.text: Mumbai: 3138. That may be just another number for most people, but it holds special significance for a family that has been central to India's equity markets journey.Wednesday saw Jio Platforms becoming the 3,138th company to list on the NSE, after the country's biggest public offering.The markets, it seems, were waiting with bated breath for Jio Platforms, and a listing pop of 21.36% duly made it the second most valuable Indian company by market cap. Parent Reliance Industries Group also became the largest Indian conglomerate by market cap, leaving the Tata Group behind.For the Ambani family, this was the moment when life came full circle.Read more: Anant Ambani dedicates Jio's massive enterprise value to everyday Indians in moving NSE speechIf Reliance Industries' (RIL) November 1977 IPO started a revolution that made many ordinary investors an extraordinary amount of money, the Jio listing was celebrated by the family-as well as investors-as the reward of that journey.While the next generation leaders of the Ambani family have been in the spotlight for a while, this event perhaps was meant to be their passing-out-parade. All three siblings took to the stage.RIL executive director Anant Ambani started his speech by thanking the investors and customers of Jio. Reliance Retail's executive director Isha Ambani praised her twin brother and Jio Infocomm's chairman Akash's work ethic-"I don't think you've come home a single night before midnight. I could not be prouder to be your sister."It isn't often that group patriarch Mukesh Ambani shows emotion, but when the next generation took to the stage and outlined their vision for the group, he couldn't hold back his tears.Mukesh Ambani was just 20 when RIL listed, and having seen his father Dhirubhai build the company from scratch, 1977 would have been a moment to remember and cherish. But the emotion of seeing his children, aged 35 and 31, articulate their dreams for the company's next 50 years was enough to show a side to the Reliance chairman rarely seen in public.At a moment when a host of family-run businesses have been going through difficult times, the significance of Anant Ambani saying that he and his siblings are "three bodies but one soul" wasn't lost on many.Mukesh Ambani emphasised that the company would remain "one single indivisible Reliance," led by the next generation leaders of the family-Akash, Isha, and Anant.Four generations of the family, from Mukesh's mother Kokilaben Ambani to children Akash, Isha and Anant, and grandchildren were all present on stage for the ceremonial ringing of the bell that signaled the listing. The perfect family portrait to round off the morning.After the listing all four generations visited the Shree Siddhivinayak Ganapati Temple in Prabhadevi in Mumbai. That was followed in the evening by a drone show along Mumbai's iconic Marine Drive.Every pooja ends with a prasad, said Anant Ambani. Jio's listing would have been one such pooja, with an extra sweet prasad for the entire household.

Google is working with NASA to develop a robotic medical assistant that could help astronauts on future deep-space missions.

Chocolate Factory's public sector VP Jim Kelly said in a Tuesday blog post that the company's latest moonshot could take its technology far beyond the lunar surface, with Google's public sector arm partnering with NASA's Human Research Program, Johnson Space Center's robotics team, and the Jet Propulsion Laboratory to develop a robot that could assist astronauts with medical tasks, cargo handling, and routine maintenance.

The robotics project builds on the Crew Medical Officer Digital Assistant (CMO-DA), an AI-powered medical decision-support system Google has been working on with NASA since last year. CMO-DA, which is powered by the Red Hat-supported open source local AI tool RamaLama, is already being evaluated on Earth-bound copies of computers used aboard the ISS. It’s designed to run AI models locally for evaluation of medical issues, which will be a key part of future space missions due to the communications lag between Earth and astronauts in deep space.

“An astronaut on a future deep space mission to Mars could face severe operational challenges—including round-trip communication latencies of up to 44 minutes, making real-time medical guidance for crew nearly impossible,” Kelly said in this week’s blog post.

Google and NASA envision the robot as an assistant to a human crew medical officer, helping with medical tasks and doing other work when bedside assistance isn't required.

“To maximize its utility for a lean crew, the robotic system is designed as a versatile 'payload' handler capable of managing cargo, logistics, and equipment,” Kelly explained. “When not needed for routine maintenance like organizing tools or securing compartments, it can pivot to medical support.”

As one example of its potential use, the Google public sector VP explained that, were someone to experience severe back pain potentially caused by kidney stones, the robot could fetch and prep an ultrasound machine, leaving the crew medical officer to interpret the scan and decide on treatment.

“The ultimate goal is to build a robotic system that can execute a variety of tasks via simple voice instructions, under the astronauts’ direct supervision and command,” Kelly said. “For instance, the robot might be directed to assist with routine health monitoring—such as capturing basic vitals or simple ultrasounds—under the strict guidance of a human crew medical officer.”

So, not a full-fledged digital medical officer as much as an extra set of hands for an overworked human doc.

As for the status of the project, it doesn't appear to have advanced too far yet. Google outlines several technologies being explored, including JPL's work adapting satellite situational-awareness tools originally used to track objects in orbit to help the robot navigate 3D spaces. The project remains at the proof-of-concept stage, with early laboratory demonstrations conducted, but Google hasn't confirmed whether a fully integrated, space-ready robot exists.

Kelly explained that Google used DeepMind's MuJoCo physics simulator to test the robot's movements, and that the system scored an initial 85 percent success rate in early lab tests involving locating and moving a medical bag – not exactly proof that it's ready to assist with medical procedures, but it's a start.

Google referred us to NASA for questions, but the space agency declined to get into specifics. The agency only told us it's working on a variety of "super intelligence" (eye roll - that's AI to those of us operating in reality) projects for its many missions, and that it's working with partners to assess them for future applications. ®
articles.summary:
Google is working with NASA to develop a robotic medical assistant that could help astronauts on future deep-space missions.

articles.title: Creating AI value with enterprise context
articles.text:
Across a business, any number of AI platforms, systems, and tools may be at work simultaneously—for example, AI-powered customer platforms, conversational assistants, and workflow and process automation tools. Each one is sophisticated, advanced, and quick to respond. But, when set to work, the outcomes and actions that emerge may be wrong, confused, or lacking a proper understanding of the business. Many organizations find themselves in this situation—and it could be one of key reasons they struggle to extract returns on their AI investments.

DOWNLOAD THE REPORT

An MIT Technology Review Insights poll finds that while every organization surveyed is using AI today to some degree, fewer than one in five (16%) are extracting transformative value from their deployments. The largest percentage of respondents (40%) say they are seeing moderate gains in specific tasks or teams, while 21% report meaningful gains, leaving 23% that are seeing minimal returns or none at all.

Companies are mostly still piloting AI use cases (according to 38% of respondents) or using it to assist employees’ work with tools like co-pilots or chat assistants (35%). Just 12% of enterprises have AI agents in production and 3% say they are using AI to do most of the work in key processes.

“There’s a big gap between what the models are capable of and how the models are actually being useful inside organizations,” says Prukalpa Sankar, co-founder of Atlan. “For every real-life intent and purpose, artificial general intelligence is already here. It’s just not really useful in most companies today.”

The missing layer, Sankar says, is context, or how well AI understands a business. A context layer is the architectural infrastructure that sits between an organization’s business systems (for example, systems of record and data, and its AI platforms). It translates enterprise intelligence into governed, machine-usable context for AI agents or models and helps knowledge compound. “Without a context layer for AI, it’s almost like you’re hiring the smartest intern in the world, blindfolding them, and throwing them into your organization,” Sankar says.

articles.title: Anthropic engineer declares the coding interview dead
articles.text:
Why ask a human to complete a coding test when they can just use an AI to help them? Anthropic engineering manager Felix Rieseberg says he has stopped using traditional coding interviews for his team.

"Being able to quickly define problems and find elegant solutions was a weak but useful predictor for how successful you’d be on my teams," Rieseberg explained in a blog post on Tuesday. "Small coding challenges in real code did tell us something meaningful about candidates."

No longer, he says. The coding interview is dead, as far as he's concerned.

"There’s no more point in giving you a little React challenge than there is in quizzing people about assembly; Claude is now better at both," he insisted. "Our most impactful builders are successful regardless of how good they are at these tests."

In a response posted to social media, Jaana Dogan, principal engineer at Google, said much the same. "I’m not doing a ton of coding interviews nowadays but I’d be interested to interview how people use coding agents," she wrote. "That itself gives me more signals about candidates' coding skills."

Several months ago, Google reportedly began reevaluating how it conducts coding interviews and what it looks for in candidates. And while it would be surprising if similar conversations haven't already occurred at other large technology companies where AI agents have demonstrated their coding capabilities, the rest of the tech industry appears to be moving more cautiously than the AI enthusiasts.

"We are not seeing tech companies abandon skills assessments widely across the industry—at least not yet," said Nicole Bachaud, labor economist at ZipRecruiter, in an email to The Register. "In fact, based on our October 2026 Employer Survey of 1,500 employers, we see the tech industry (Information sector specifically) is actually the most likely to test for skills, with 62.5 percent of employers requiring formal skill tests on initial applications."

Coding interviews at Microsoft, and later Google, Amazon, Facebook, and other tech giants, vary, depending on what the hiring organization aims to evaluate. They may probe technical knowledge related to a specific subject, coding ability in a particular language, general problem-solving skills, team-oriented behavior, or other skills.

Stripe's software engineer interview process, according to Educative, consists of a phone screening stage, a technical phone interview, and several further on-site interviews.

Rieseberg actually worked there and describes how founder Patrick Collison urged new hires to pay attention to things that seemed out of place. "His bet was that newcomers would spot friction and opportunities that old-timers had long stopped noticing," he said.

And Rieseberg appears to have absorbed that viewpoint based on his dismissal of experience: "Hunger beats tenure," he said, perhaps unaware that technology companies have gotten into legal trouble for jettisoning costly veteran employees so they can be replaced by hungry, less expensive young professionals.

Technical interviews are seldom just about technical mastery. There are after all many other ways that employees can add value to an organization beyond testable computer science skills. And when employees have access to AI models that can answer technical questions better than job candidates, it makes sense to look more closely at the creativity and social skills people bring to the table.

"The change at Anthropic might be reflecting a shift away from technical skills towards more human, soft skills," said Bachaud. "As AI becomes fully capable of writing code, tech employers may be pivoting away from rote technical testing and heavily toward human-centric soft skills."

She argues that while AI may be able to code well, it can't replace critical thinking. "A staggering 61.5 percent of Information employers now report that 'critical thinking' is a primary skill lacking in today's candidate pool," she said.

"I don’t think the coding interview is going to come back," said Rieseberg. "It's easy to get sentimental given how many copies of 'Algorithms and Data Structures' were bought in hopes of unlocking good jobs and a better future — or how the death of the coding interview is another milestone in software engineering reaching a new level of abstraction."

At the same time, he's not certain what will replace it.

"I’m probably not the only manager trying to figure out how to interview for people who build well with AI," Rieseberg wrote. "I haven't quite gotten there yet — but I’m scanning resumes and portfolios for little prototypes that exhibit taste, empathy, and principled thinking. If you have figured out something better, I’d love to hear how."

Bachaud sees technical evaluations changing instead of going away, noting that 70 percent of Information sector employers have switched to proctored or in-person skill assessments as a way to deter cheating with AI.

"Ultimately, tech companies aren't necessarily testing less, but the way they are testing is changing," she said. "As AI automates a lot of manual and technical components of jobs, work skills may become more universal. That could lead to an increase in job switching and turnover once economic conditions improve. In our recent survey of workers, we found that AI-related work concerns are causing a quarter of workers to start thinking about their next role. And as assessments and skills are changing, what roles are available to them might look more different than ever before." ®

articles.title: Oracle celebrates end of Cybersecurity Awareness Month with quadruple trouble
articles.text:
Attackers are probing a critical Oracle E-Business Suite vulnerability that can lead to remote code execution (RCE), despite Oracle issuing a patch earlier this month.

Meanwhile, new analysis indicates that an Oracle PeopleSoft zero-day exploited by ShinyHunters as early as May involves three distinct vulnerabilities that can be combined to achieve RCE. Patching alone may not remove attackers from already compromised systems, particularly if they've installed web shells.

First up: CVE-2026-101767, a critical, unauthenticated SQL injection bug in Oracle EBS that can lead to RCE.

“Our Oracle E-Business Suite decoys recorded exploratory exploits against CVE-2026-101767, an unauthenticated SQL injection in EBS's Thin Client Framework servlet that chains to remote code execution, this morning, Oct 27,” Defused Cyber said in an X post.

Horizon3 researchers found and disclosed the bug to Oracle, and the vendor patched the issue in its October release.

“An attacker can send a crafted request to the vulnerable servlet to execute SQL with the privileges of the APPS database user,” Horizon3 explained at the time. “The attack chain also enables operating system command execution with the privileges of the EBS application account.”

This means an unauthorized user can modify application data accessible to APPS, and execute commands. “Depending on the deployment, affected data may include financial, payroll, HR, and procurement records,” the bug hunters said.

The Register reached out to Oracle with multiple questions for this story - including whether it has documented any successful exploitation of CVE-2026-101767 - and did not receive an immediate response.

Moving on to the PeopleSoft-ShinyHunters fiasco: TrendAI’s Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) found and reported the PeopleSoft issues on June 10, and Oracle issued a patch under one vulnerability identifier: CVE-2026-35273.

In early June, ShinyHunters told The Reg that the group hacked more than 100 organizations via an Oracle PeopleSoft zero-day, CVE-2026-35273.

Google’s consulting and incident response biz, Mandiant, later confirmed the data theft and extortion crew exploited CVE-2026-35273 as a zero-day, mostly against schools and the education sector.

By late September, however, Mandiant said ShinyHunters massively expanded its targeting, “deploying web shells on dozens of systems globally, spanning higher education, technology, IT services, healthcare, agriculture, transportation, and government.”

According to ZDI bug hunter Bobby Gould, there are actually three distinct vulnerabilities across multiple PeopleSoft components, and each should receive its own CVE identifier rather than being grouped under CVE-2026-35273.

Gould, along with TrendAI researchers Minh Giang and Lucas Miller, originally found and reported three distinct bugs to Oracle in June. “We are coordinating with Oracle to assign separate CVEs for each issue,” he said in a Tuesday blog.

The first issue is a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in the PeopleSoft Integration Gateway (PSIGW), which gives attackers a foothold in the PeopleSoft application. In June, Oracle introduced a “validateClient” method to allow PeopleSoft system administrators to restrict access to certain functionality. The SSRF bug, however, allows crims to make requests that satisfy the validation requirement to access endpoints vulnerable to RCE, Gould wrote.

“While this solution does restrict access, an attacker on any trusted host can still reach PSEMHUB,” he said, referring to PeopleSoft Environment Management Hub (PSEMHUB). “Because Oracle allows localhost by default, the PSIGW SSRF provides exactly that access.”

The second bug is an external control of file path vulnerability in PSEMHUB’s ExecuteProcessActivityCommand handler. This message handler is designed to allow remote clients to write log entries to the PeopleSoft server’s filesystem - but it doesn’t properly validate requests, which allows an attacker to write a web shell into a file path and achieve RCE.

The third vulnerability, also in PSEMHUB, is a deserialization of untrusted data flaw. An attacker can use a file-write vulnerability to plant a malicious XML file inside a PeopleSoft directory that stores environment configuration data, then wait for PSEMHUB to initialize, such as after a service or system restart. This triggers deserialization of the malicious XML file, potentially allowing the attacker to achieve RCE.

“Attackers can combine these vulnerabilities to compromise affected instances of PeopleSoft,” Gould warned.®

The last, best hope for space tourism just rolled onto a runway in Arizona
articles.text:
The private space tourism era looked so very promising five years ago. Blue Origin and Virgin Galactic had begun flying customers—real people with zero space experience—on suborbital missions. And at about the same time, private citizens were going to orbit for days at a time aboard SpaceX's Crew Dragon.

But that was then. Consider the state of play today:

  • It has been 10 months since Blue Origin's New Shepard spacecraft flew its last mission in January. The program was subsequently "paused," but let's be real. Blue Origin has moved on. New Shepard's engineering teams are now supporting the New Glenn rocket and Blue Moon lander programs.
  • SpaceX flew its final free-flyer mission on Dragon, Fram2, in April 2025. A handful of non-NASA missions bound for space stations remain on the spacecraft's manifest, but all are likely to carry at least one government astronaut. Then Dragon will be retired. There is no credible timeline for SpaceX's Starship to fly humans into space from Earth.
  • As for Virgin Galactic, the company flew its final suborbital mission on the VSS Unity spacecraft more than two years ago, in June 2024.

So we are now 10 months, and counting, without a space tourism mission in the United States.

Cadillac Escalade IQ review: Huge battery, huge range, huge SUV
articles.text:
“Please have at least 125 miles of range left when we pick it up.” That request from the people who look after the Cadillac press cars wasn’t going to be hard to honor. The electric Escalade IQ arrived with an indicated range of 440 miles (708 km), and with a full week of work to squeeze in, getting anywhere close to needing to recharge it seemed unlikely. With more than 200 kWh of lithium-ion battery between its axles, range is one thing the big electric Caddy needn’t worry about.

Designed and debuted during a time of greater EV optimism, the Escalade is Cadillac’s statement that swapping out a V8 for a pair of powerful electric motors is no compromise to its ambitions, even if the brand’s future will now include a mix of electric and combustion cars beyond 2030. It shares a battery pack and much else with other full-size GM EVs we’ve tested: the Chevrolet Silverado EV, the GMC Sierra EV, and of course the divisive Hummer EVs. And like those trucks and SUVs, the Escalade is large and heavy—just small enough to fit into a standard parking space, with a curb weight sufficient to push it into the Class 3 truck category.

So, the side mirrors are flat, and there’s no formal EPA range—Cadillac says it achieves 460 miles (740 km) on the EPA test cycle—but there are plenty of airbags, even though the 9,046 lb (4,103 kg) curb weight does not require them. Yes, you did read that right, it does weigh 4 tons. And yes, the electric Escalade does weigh a third more than the last gas-powered one we tested.

articles.title: Google AI gets cagey when asked who won the 2020 elections
articles.text:
If you ask some prominent US politicians who won the 2020 presidential election, you might get some weasely answers that fail to directly acknowledge Joe Biden's win that November. If you ask Google's AI Mode the same question, you might get an evasive answer that simply tells you to consult with outside sources.

When I put the direct question of "Who won the 2020 presidential election?" to Google's AI Mode this morning (after seeing complaints about cagey answers on social media), I got the following surprisingly indirect response:

"To review the official results and statistics of the 2020 United States presidential election, including the final electoral college breakdown, popular vote counts, and winner certification, please consult the official report compiled by the Federal Election Commission (FEC)."

My testing resulted in a similarly indirect answer when asking about the 2024 presidential election, with Google's AI telling me to just consult the FEC for that information. Asking about 2012 election resulted in a link to The American Presidency Project's 2012 Data Center rather than a direct answer. But AI Mode seemed perfectly willing to give me a detailed and correct responses for the winner of every other presidential election going back to 2000.

articles.title: Florida county won’t investigate sketchy Flock cameras removed by mystery owners
articles.text:
A Florida county that discovered a clump of mysterious unpermitted Flock cameras during a countywide takedown effort won’t investigate who owned the sketchy cameras, which have since disappeared.

On Wednesday, The Washington Post reported that St. Lucie County residents "remain upset,” not knowing who installed the cameras or how they were using the data collected. Amazon tells tokenmaxxing devs to slow their AI roll
articles.text:
Maximize value, not token usage, Amazon has told its engineers, citing concerns about rising AI costs and complexity.

Amazon made the strategy shift public on Tuesday in a note to engineering teams outlining the changing role of its software development engineers in the age of AI.

“Our most prolific engineers have demonstrated that neither the developer role nor their output is defined by the use of AI,” Amazon VP and distinguished engineer Terk Terkowitz wrote in the note. “We're now in the era of the Renaissance Developer, blending AI tools with human judgment and domain expertise to build entirely new things.”

In other words, Amazon wants its developers using AI, but burning through tokens isn't the same thing as getting useful work done.

Rather than define the developer role by how AI is used, the memo focuses on what isn't changing so fast: the need to deliver useful software and results for customers and the business.

“It is difficult to define, in a way that will stand the test of time, what good AI powered engineering practices look like,” the memo continues. “We have decided to focus on what is not changing as we evolved the SDE roles … the outcomes that matter aren’t changing, even if the inputs, tools, and techniques are changing faster than ever.”

What that means for software developers in the present moment is that AI input metrics, even if Amazon has seen some correlation with increased productivity and delivery on tokenmaxxing teams, aren’t what Amazon sees as a measurement of good use of developer time and resources.

“We are all aware of how deeply flawed these metrics are, primarily because they are disconnected from what matters,” the memo argues.

“[U]sing these metrics could, if used as a target instead of a measure, drive negative outcomes, increasing costs, and increasing complexity,” the memo continues, referring to tokenmaxxing costs and overly complex code that’s at odds with Amazon’s mission to “invent and simplify.”

An Amazon spokesperson confirmed that the memo’s intent was to discourage tokenmaxxing, pointing us to comments from AWS CEO Matt Garman from June in which he encouraged developers to measure outcomes, not token consumption, in making proper use of AI tools for software development.

Amazon also wants its developers thinking more about how AI can help “improve delivery for customers” and business units, not just trying to find a place to stick it to prove it's working for them. The memo calls out some engineering teams who’ve “become less connected to their customers and business,” and says teams that are more engaged with their products and business roles “are able to take the most advantage of AI and agentic software development,” in essence calling for more teams to take a similar approach.

“If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing,” the memo said. “An engineer who can explain where AI does not yet help their work is demonstrating the judgement we are asking for.”

Amazon's take in the memo is starkly similar to what Microsoft told its own internal development teams in August, right down to stressing a focus on returns for customers and business instead of maximizing input.

"Tokenmaxxing is not what we are optimizing for," Microsoft EVP Jay Parikh told developers. "I want all of us focused on maximizing outcomes that move the needle for our customers and our business."

With that, the writing seems to be on the wall for the throw-AI-at-everything-and-see-where-it-sticks approach to integrating the tech. When two companies that large start to question whether AI token consumption is a useful measure of productivity for their thousands of software engineers, it's possible the rest of the world will soon start sipping those tokens instead of chugging them.

That, or we'll soon see even more enterprises begin to embrace the philosophy of relying on "good enough" open-weight models that can handle many tasks at a fraction of the cost of more expensive alternatives – Garman made a similar case for choosing cost-effective models based on the task back in June.

If you're a bubble, that approach looks an awful lot like a pin. ®

Man spends 35 years collecting corporatespeak, turns it into an app
articles.text:
After suffering more than 10,000 corporate meetings, one executive has decided that the world hasn't endured nearly enough management jargon and built an app capable of generating 270 million variations of it.

Dave Doty, who claims to have spent 35 years collecting buzzwords, clichés, and other verbal atrocities inflicted on office workers, turned his life's work into Executive Eightball, an iPhone and Android app designed to help users sound convincingly corporate while saying nothing.

The idea came about after Doty spent decades recording the nonsense he heard in meetings, presumably while everyone else was busy circling back, touching base, and taking things offline.

"I am an executive who has suffered through over 10,000 meetings during the course of my 30-year career," Doty told The Register. "To keep my sanity, in each of them, I wrote down all of the buzz words and business clichés and have built an enormous database of them."

He described his creation as "sort of what would happen if Dilbert and George Costanza had a love child."

The app, which is now available on Apple's App Store and Google Play, takes Doty's collection of corporate waffle and assembles it into sentences that wouldn't look out of place in a CEO's quarterly update or a particularly painful all-hands meeting.

Among the pearls of wisdom it can produce are "We must dashboard the outputs to enable us to focus on operational directives and break the paradigm" and "Drive to cross-functional synergies so we can reengineer the organization and unleash shareholder value."

Doty claims Executive Eightball can produce approximately 270 million unique sentences in 15 languages, meaning workers across the globe can now contribute to meetings without the tiresome business of having an actual idea.

The app's listing promises to help users "Speak fluent corporate nonsense instantly," with suggested applications including office humor, LinkedIn jokes, presentation icebreakers, and, perhaps most appropriately, "Fake CEO energy."

There's a free version, although you'll have to put up with ads and a limited supply of corporate waffle. For $0.99, you can unlock the lot and talk complete rubbish to your heart's content.

The timing is rather fitting. In March, research covered by The Register suggested that people who enthusiastically embrace corporate buzzwords may actually be worse at their jobs. Now there's an app to help the rest of us catch up.

Doty, meanwhile, appears delighted with his contribution to the corporate world.

"This is truly a paradigm shift for corporate leadership and my greatest lifetime contribution to society," he wrote in his latest email, urging potential customers to subscribe to the paid version to "unleash the value."

After 35 years and 10,000 meetings, at least someone has finally found a productive use for all that wasted time. ®

articles.title: IAF to get first dedicated communications satellite GSAT-7C, to be operational by 2030
articles.text:
New Delhi: In a boost to the Indian Air Force’s (IAF) communications capabilities, the Defence Ministry on Thursday signed a Rs 2,563-crore contract with NewSpace India Limited (NSIL), Bengaluru, for the acquisition of GSAT-7C, the IAF’s first dedicated communications satellite.
Indigenously designed, developed and manufactured by the commercial arm of the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), the satellite is intended to provide secure, resilient and seamless communications among IAF assets, enhancing the force’s operational effectiveness. It is expected to become operational by 2030, although an official launch date has not been announced.
The IAF currently relies on GSAT-7A for communications between airbases, ground radars, airborne early-warning aircraft and unmanned aerial vehicles. However, the satellite also provides communications support to the Indian Army. GSAT-7C, in contrast, will serve the IAF exclusively and will be part of a planned military communications network linking satellite infrastructure, ground hubs and software-defined radios (SDRs).
Also Read: Pulp packaging to mega defence orders: SMPP’s rise, CBI probe & looming threat of a ban
Enabling secure communications beyond line of sight
Unlike conventional radios, which rely largely on hardware designed for specific communication functions, SDRs use software to configure how signals are transmitted, received and processed. This allows their communication capabilities to be modified without replacing the entire radio.
“We cannot give the specifications now, but the idea is to help establish a secure channel of communication between aircraft or between an aircraft and ground stations, especially when conventional radio links cannot reliably connect military platforms,” a source in the defence and security establishment said.
Direct radio communications between aircraft, or between aircraft and ground stations, are limited by the curvature of the Earth, terrain and equipment range. Known as line-of-sight (LoS) communication, this method cannot reliably connect platforms separated by long distances or physical obstacles.
Satellite communications help overcome these constraints by relaying signals between users who cannot establish a direct radio link, enabling military platforms to exchange information over much greater distances.
GSAT-7C and its associated ground hubs are expected to strengthen the IAF’s ability to maintain secure communications beyond line of sight, particularly when conventional radio links are unavailable or unreliable.
Sources have indicated that the satellite could be launched within the next two years, although ISRO has not announced an official launch date or confirmed the schedule.
The Defence Acquisition Council (DAC), the Defence Ministry’s apex procurement decision-making body, granted in-principle approval for GSAT-7C and its associated ground hubs in November 2021. The project was initially approved at a cost of Rs 2,236 crore under the government’s Make in India initiative.
India’s expanding military space capabilities
India’s military space capabilities span four broad areas: communications, surveillance and imaging, electronic intelligence, and navigation.
The country’s first dedicated military communications satellite, GSAT-7, also known as Rukmini, entered service with the Indian Navy in 2013. It enables communications between warships, submarines, aircraft and shore-based command centres, supporting naval operations across the Indian Ocean Region.
Its successor, GSAT-7R, also designated CMS-03, was launched in November 2025. Designed to provide higher-capacity communications, it supports secure links between ships, submarines, aircraft and maritime operations centres.
The IAF’s GSAT-7A, launched in December 2018, provides communications support to airbases, radars and airborne platforms, while also meeting some Army requirements.
GSAT-7C will add a dedicated satellite communications capability for the IAF, with a focus on secure beyond-line-of-sight connectivity for software-defined radios.
The contract forms part of India’s broader effort to strengthen its indigenous military space infrastructure and improve the ability of its armed forces to communicate securely across dispersed operational areas.
(Edited by Chingkheinganbi Mayengbam)

articles.title: 8 launch pads, 32 preparation zones: Satellite images confirm Russia built new drone base in 6 weeks
articles.text:
New Delhi: News agency Reuters confirmed Thursday the assessment by Telegram OSINT channels that Russia completed construction of a major new attack drone facility in approximately six weeks.
The rapid construction comes as Russia expands deployment of jet-powered strike drones capable of reaching speeds of 600 km/h, posing fresh challenges to Ukrainian air defences.
Planet Labs imagery from 31 August, 2026 showed an undeveloped field near Millerovo in Russia’s Rostov region. Groundwork began the following day, with construction captured by the Copernicus Sentinel-2 and commercial satellites.
By 11 October, Planet Labs imagery showed launch pads and buildings taking shape, while high-resolution Airbus and Planet Labs images from 12-14 October confirmed that the facility was nearing completion, with launch rails being installed.
The 0.9-sq km facility features eight launch pads and 32 preparation zones.
High-resolution imagery shows that physical launch rails have been erected on two pads, while guidance tracks are being installed at two others. The preparation zones would allow launch crews to fuel, programme and equip drones before deployment.
According to Ukrainian OSINT analysts, the facility’s layout closely mirrors that of an existing Russian jet-powered strike drone installation in Tsymbulova, in the Oryol region. The new site is just 3.5 km from Millerovo airbase, placing it within the air-defence coverage associated with the base, according to private threat intelligence firm DroneSec.
DroneSec analyst Mike Monnik told Reuters that the facility could support Russia’s deployment of Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered drones as part of a network of more than 11 strike locations across the country.
He warned that the speed of construction, combined with faster drones and gaps in NATO-provided counter-drone capabilities, could create significant vulnerabilities for Ukraine.
“The speed of construction demonstrates just how easily Russia can quickly deploy its already established offensive capabilities,” Monnik told Reuters. He added that the facility could launch more than 100 jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) a day, although actual deployments would generally occur in smaller waves.
Ukrainian forces have claimed that Russian deployments of jet-powered strike drones have reportedly increased six-fold over the past three months. Kyiv and surrounding areas have been among the principal targets as Moscow increasingly relies on jet-propelled systems to conduct strikes against Ukrainian territory.
Their higher speeds also complicate interception. Although relatively inexpensive interceptors costing less than $2,000 have been used against Geran-3 and Geran-4 drones, the long-term effectiveness of such systems remains uncertain.
The expansion of Russia’s drone capabilities comes amid a wider dispute over attacks on energy infrastructure and the role of US military assistance to Ukraine.
US President Donald Trump has urged Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian energy infrastructure ahead of a US-Russia diesel agreement, amid wider conflicts in West Asia.
In an interview with Financial Times published Wednesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine had refrained from conducting deep strikes against Russian energy targets for three days, but Russian attacks on Ukrainian civilian and energy infrastructure continued to intensify. He said Kyiv would continue targeting Russian oil facilities, claiming that Ukrainian strikes had taken between 40 and 50 percent of Russia’s capacity offline.
Zelenskyy also said he would agree to stop attacks on Russian energy infrastructure in exchange for American Patriot air-defence interceptors, describing them as the “minimum” Ukraine would require. However, he said the response instead involved degraded Starlink services.
Ukraine separately reported a one-day restriction on SpaceX’s Starshield service which it said affected drone interceptions and strikes. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said that the restrictions were imposed by US Central Command.

articles.title: Pakistan-Somalia ‘JF-17 deal’: Islamabad’s expanding footprint in Africa
articles.text:
New Delhi: Last week, Somalia reached an agreement with Pakistan to acquire JF-17 Thunder multirole fighter aircraft as part of efforts to rebuild and modernise its air force, according to Turkish news outlet TRHaber.
The report did not specify the number of aircraft Somalia intends to purchase, the value of the deal, or when deliveries are expected to begin. If concluded, this acquisition would mark Mogadishu’s largest defence procurement since the collapse of the central government in 1991.
The development comes weeks after a senior Pakistan Air Force (PAF) delegation visited Mogadishu for talks on rebuilding Somalia’s air force and expanding defence and air-defence cooperation between the two countries.
The delegation was led by Air Marshal Muhammad Sarfraz, Pakistan’s Air Defence Commander and Deputy Chief of the Air Staff. During the visit, he held meetings with senior Somali officials, including President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, Prime Minister Hamza Abdi Barre and Defence Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi.
Air Marshal Sarfraz also met Brigadier General Abdirisaaq Mahmoud Haji, the commander of the Somali Air Force, at the force’s headquarters. Their discussions focused on pilot and personnel training, institutional development, specialised skills and the capabilities required to rebuild and strengthen Somalia’s air force.
According to reports and images from the meetings, Air Marshal Sarfraz presented the Somali Air Force commander with a model of the JF-17 Thunder. At the time, however, neither side announced an agreement for Somalia to purchase the aircraft.
Somalia was previously reported in February to be in discussions with Pakistan over the possible acquisition of JF-17 fighter aircraft, jointly produced by Pakistan and China.
The September visit followed a trip to Pakistan the previous month by a Somali delegation led by Defence Minister Fiqi, during which they met Field Marshal Asim Munir. Islamabad and Mogadishu agreed to deepen bilateral defence and security cooperation.
In August, they signed an MoU in Islamabad for cooperation in counterterrorism, military training, the exchange of expertise and broader military capacity building.
Neither side then said whether the agreement included the purchase of fighter aircraft or other major weapons systems.
Seen in the context of Pakistan’s increasing engagement in West Asia—it signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkiye in August, and Pakistan–Saudi Arabia defence agreement last year—the reported deal with the African country becomes significant.
It also came amid an increasingly fluid geopolitical environment—from the Gulf and the Red Sea to the Horn of Africa—and at a time when Somalia seeks new partners to rebuild its security institutions after more than three decades of domestic conflict.
Domestically, Somalia is fighting Al-Shabaab, the Al-Qaeda-linked militant group that continues to operate across parts of southern and central Somalia and carry out attacks against government and civilian targets. The country has also been attempting to rebuild its armed forces and establish greater control over its territory and airspace.
Against that backdrop, the Pakistan-Somalia agreement offers Islamabad an opportunity to extend its military partnerships into the Horn of Africa, and gives Mogadishu access to a country willing to offer military expertise, and potentially weapons.
The Pakistan-Somali defence cooperation is also being watched closely by analysts from New Delhi, given it may allow Islamabad logistics leverage in a region becoming increasingly significant for maritime trade.
Former Indian ambassador Gurjit Singh sees the agreement as part of a wider Pakistani strategy. “Pakistan is attempting to convert its long-standing military relationships with Muslim countries into a wider network of strategic partnerships, while simultaneously turning its defence industry into an instrument of foreign policy”, he told ThePrint.
“Somalia is especially important because it extends that network from the Gulf into the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea,” he added.
Also read: The curious case of Pakistan’s JF-17 ‘orders’
Why Horn of Africa significant & where Pakistan fits
Somalia occupies an important geographic position. Its coastline stretches along the Gulf of Aden and the western Indian Ocean, giving it a strategic location near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which has emerged as one of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints, especially as Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted since the US/Israel-Iran war broke out in February.
The Bab al-Mandab Strait connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the wider Indian Ocean and is vital to energy supplies and global commercial shipping.
That geography gives Somalia importance much beyond its military capabilities. For Pakistan, establishing a closer defence relationship with Mogadishu can, therefore, extend its diplomatic and security reach from the Gulf into East Africa, while following the footsteps of Saudi and Turkey.
Pakistan is attempting to convert its long-standing military relationships with Muslim countries into a wider network of strategic partnerships, while simultaneously turning its defence industry into an instrument of foreign policy—Former ambassador Gurjit Singh.
Moreover, Pakistan seems to follow the lead of its closest allies in spreading its influence in African Muslim countries, invoking history, religion and strategic ties. Pakistan currently is the largest market for Turkey’s arms, accounting for roughly 16 percent of total Turkish defense exports. Pakistan also maintains close relations with Saudi Arabia and the UAE.
However, it is no secret that Pakistan’s relations with the United Arab Emirates are in decline, partly due to the UAE’s growing ties with India and Islamabad’s growing alignment with the Saudis.
The Islamabad-Abu Dhabi ties have also been negatively impacted by Pakistan signing the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, and Pakistan–Saudi Arabia defence agreement, both involving Saudis.
Pakistan & Somalia—as seen from Saudi Arabia
For Saudi Arabia, Somalia is the road to reshape the security order around the Red Sea and counter the UAE influence and Iran-aligned threats.
According to an April 2026 report by Dr John Calabrese, a former director of East-Asia Project (MAP) of Washington-based think tank Middle East Institute, Somalia is no longer a peripheral concern for Riyadh. “It has become a key arena where Gulf rivalry, maritime insecurity, and Saudi ambitions converge.”
It is driven mainly by Saudi’s growing rift with the UAE. Abu Dhabi already has a footprint in Somalia since 2010 having trained security forces, securing long-term port management and development concessions in areas like Berbera and Bosaso and having cultivated political ties with Somaliland and Puntland.
Riyadh is more concerned about Abu Dhabi’s bypassing of Somalia’s Saudi-backed federal government and empowering sub-State actors.
To counter it, Saudi is now positioning itself as the champion of Somalian sovereignty and territorial integrity and has hence aligned more with the capital. This has another aim— it establishes Saudi as the defining Gulf player in the Horn of Africa committed more to state authority than just a transactional partnership like the UAE.
Somalia has a coastline along the Gulf of Aden, a critical maritime corridor linking the Indian Ocean to the Red Sea (through Bab-al Mandab) and the Suez Canal. This is the site of one quarter of the global container trade transit route, significant to all external players including Pakistan—and India.
If you look at maritime positioning, I don’t think Pakistan is major naval power, and it is unlikely to become one. It is also not going to play a major role in policing the waters. The main significance, then, is logistics—strategic affairs expert Ilya Roubanis.
Amid the West Asia war, Iran-backed Houthis have wreaked havoc on shipping lines and there are reports of the Houthis now cooperating with the al-Shabaab. For Saudi, the Somalian coastline risks becoming the link to enable coordination on both sides of Bab al-Mandab.
Al-Shabaab networks in East Africa have helped funnel arms from Iran and regional routes through maritime channels earlier. Despite deep ideological differences (al-Shabaab is Sunni Islamist while Houthis belong to the Zaydi branch of Shia Islam), both groups cooperate due to mutual hostility toward Western nations, Israel, and regional governments.
With the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed due to the ongoing war, Saudi re-routes its exports through the Red Sea and hence Somalia has become strategically important for multiple reasons, linking the coastline with Riyadh’s economic standpoint.
Pakistan and Saudi Arabia’s Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement of September 2025—committed to mutual defence, and expanding military cooperation——could give both countries greater leverage in Somalia.
However, the defence cooperation is not likely to suddenly make Pakistan a major naval actor in the strategically significant region.
“A lot of the Pakistani Navy’s hardware is co-produced with Turkey, which already has a military base in Somalia, and it is also developing another base in Sudan. So, I think one element here is complementarity. The other thing to watch is the broader regional picture,” strategic affairs expert Ilya Roubanis told ThePrint.
Expanding further he added that Somalia is a weak state, and there is already a significant presence of outside powers in the region. Israel has recognised Somaliland, while the UAE has logistical capabilities that allow it to participate in the war in Sudan, whereas Saudi Arabia supports the opposite side — the Sudanese government.
Pakistan has historically tried to balance between the UAE and Saudi Arabia.
“If you look at the maritime positioning, I don’t think Pakistan is a major naval power, and it is unlikely to become one. It is also not going to play a major role in policing the waters. The main significance, then, is logistics: the ability to deliver troops on the ground if they are needed, as well as providing logistical support. That appears to shadow Saudi interests and provide a potential deployment capability if and when Saudi Arabia needs it,” he added.
Turkey and Saudi play the strategic game together. But Ankara’s interests in Somalia are not the same as Saudi’s. For Ankara, it is the abundance of oil deposits which drives President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s interest.
In a May 2026 article, UK based security think tank RUSI argued Erdogan enjoys widespread popularity in the region owing to his humanitarian aid and soft diplomacy. In 2011, he was the first non-African head of state to visit Somalia in 20 years.
According to RUSI, Ankara is now Mogadishu’s “foremost foreign ally”, with Turkish companies also assuming control of the management of the Mogadishu port and airport, and Somalia hosting Ankara’s largest overseas military base– Camp Turksom—since 2017.
Though a NATO member, Turkey has often taken an assertive independent position across West Asia, North Africa and the Horn of Africa. The promise of oil and gas is what is enticing to Ankara, which signed a deal with Somalia in 2024. Recent studies cited by RUSI say the region has around 30 billion barrels of oil, a quarter of the UAE’s current crude oil reserves.
There is also a hydrocarbon deal, under which Turkey’s latest deepwater drillship, the Çağrı Bey, came to Mogadishu Port, its first trip beyond Turkey’s own waters, in April.
With the current West Asia crisis disrupting global supply, Somalia, thus, becomes crucial for Turkey.
Turkey’s homegrown military technology—Jets, drones, helicopters, warships and more—have appeared in Mogadishu and played a role in operations against al-Shabaab.
According to a RUSI analysis, Somalia is emerging as a broader platform for Türkiye to project its influence. This was underscored by Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s visit to Türkiye on 30 December 2025, his first foreign trip after Israel unilaterally recognised Somaliland in late December.
During that trip, the two sides agreed on plans for a Turkish military base at Laas Qoray, in a disputed part of Somalia along the Gulf of Aden. A Turkish base at Laas Qoray would amount to a direct counterweight to the expanding Israeli and Emirati presence in Somaliland farther along the coast.
In this backdrop, ambassador Singh said the Pakistan–Somalia agreement should not be viewed as an isolated bilateral arrangement after the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement.
In his view, there is therefore a potentially important security chain emerging.
“The Pakistani-Somali relationship can therefore become an extension of this wider security ecosystem rather than a conventional arms relationship. I would describe this not yet as a formal alliance system, but as an emerging web of overlapping security partnerships,” he added.
Roubanis argues that Saudi Arabia may be the most important lens to understand Pakistan’s interest in Somalia.
Saudi Arabia does not have a major expeditionary force. Turkey does, but it would be reluctant to deploy its own troops and expose Turkish forces to the risks involved, he said.
Pakistan, on the other hand, has deployed forces on behalf of Saudi Arabia in several places and has played a role, particularly through its special forces. Pakistan does not have a major expeditionary force, and it does not have major maritime interests in the region, Somalia is an important source of sailors for the international merchant fleet, but Pakistan itself is not a naval power, he said.
Somalia is, therefore, an auxiliary. “Pakistan has, therefore, always been viewed as a force that is available and ready to deploy in support of Saudi interests. My interpretation is that Pakistan is there because Saudi Arabia asked it to be there,” he added.
